# Why simulation studies

Simulation is the basic experimental practice of statistical research --- the
equivalent of basic lab skills in the bench sciences. Its purpose follows from a
single observation: to evaluate a method objectively, we must know what the right
answer is, and for real data we never do. So we create artificial data where the
truth is known, apply the methods to it, and compare the results against that
known truth.

This control over the data-generating model is what makes simulation
indispensable. It lets us

1. determine how accurate methods are and which perform best, because the truth
   is known;
2. trace how performance changes as a function of sample size, signal strength,
   dimension, and other parameters;
3. study how sensitive methods are to their assumptions, by deliberately
   generating data in which those assumptions are violated.

Simulation plays a role in every kind of statistical research. In **applied**
work it justifies the choice of a particular method for the analysis at hand. In
**methodological** work it demonstrates numerically that a new method improves on
its competitors. In **computational** work it demonstrates improved accuracy or
speed. In **theoretical** work it validates numerically what the theory predicts.
A typical statistics paper devotes an entire section to it, between Method and
Data Analysis, and the supplement carries the code that reproduces it.

Comparisons can themselves be the research product: a careful study informing the
community about the relative advantages of existing methods is a contribution
even when no new method is developed.

### Three kinds of data in simulations

**Artificial data** is generated from a pre-specified statistical model chosen in
the context of the methodological question. This is the default meaning of
"simulated data" and the focus of this guide.

**Real data** can also serve, when methods can be evaluated by model-agnostic
measures --- split the data into a training part for fitting and a test part for
evaluation, then compare classification or prediction accuracy on the test set.

**Perturbed data** is real data artificially disturbed, used to study how
robust a method's results are to perturbation.

### Replications

For each fixed design, data is generated many times. Replication accounts for
the variability in a method's performance, and a single draw tells you almost
nothing. More replications give more confidence in the comparison at a higher
computational cost --- §4.4 makes this trade-off precise.

The consequence worth internalizing early: simulation results are *estimates*,
computed from a finite number of replications, and carry uncertainty of their
own. A study reporting a difference of 0.02 between two methods without
quantifying the noise in that 0.02 has not established anything.

# The four components

Every simulation study has the same four components. Working through them in
order, in writing, before any substantial coding, is what separates a study that
answers its question from one that merely produces output.

| Component | The questions it answers |
|---|---|
| **Goal** | What is the context and aim of the comparison? |
| **Design** | Which methods? Which data-generating mechanism, with which parameters? Which performance measures? How many replications? |
| **Implementation** | Functions for data generation, methods, and metrics; scripts to run the simulation and save results; scripts to turn results into tables and figures; scripts applying the methods to real data |
| **Summary** | How are the results communicated in the presentation and the written report? |

: The four components of a simulation study {tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

Readers coming from the published literature will recognize this as a
practically-organized version of the **ADEMP** framework of Morris, White, and
Crowther (2019) --- Aims, Data-generating mechanisms, Estimands, Methods,
Performance measures. ADEMP is an excellent checklist for *reporting* a study;
the four components above are organized around *doing* one, which is why
Implementation appears as a first-class concern here.

# Goal

State the claim, not the activity. "Compare several methods for linear
regression" is an activity. A goal is specific about three things:

- **the method type** --- e.g. linear regression of a response $y$ on $p$
  covariates $x_1, \dots, x_p$;
- **the specifics** --- e.g. situations where $p$ is large, possibly larger than
  the sample size $n$, and where not all variables are important;
- **the motivation** --- e.g. modern biological datasets are often
  high-dimensional (1000 genes, 100 samples), and it is biologically plausible
  that not all genes are needed for prediction.

Stated this way, the goal already constrains the design: if the motivation is
$p > n$ with few important variables, then $p > n$ scenarios and sparse
coefficient vectors are not optional.

# Design

## Which methods to pick

Selecting the methods is itself a research task requiring a genuine literature
search. Three criteria make a candidate viable:

1. **It falls within the area of interest** defined by the goal.
2. **It has a ready implementation** in R (or whichever language the study uses).
   A method you must implement from scratch is a project of its own.
3. **It is well described** in textbooks or articles, so that its assumptions and
   inputs can be understood rather than guessed at.

For the high-dimensional regression example, this yields forward selection,
ridge regression, lasso, and principal component regression --- each designed to
function when $p > n$, each with a mature R implementation, each covered in
standard references.

Study each method's implementation closely enough to know its inputs, its
outputs, and what it does *not* provide. Discovering mid-study that a method
returns loadings but no scores, or requires a tuning parameter you have not
planned to choose, is expensive.

> **Tuning is part of the method.** If the lasso penalty is chosen by 5-fold
> cross-validation, then "lasso + 5-fold CV" is what is being evaluated. Giving
> one competitor an oracle-tuned parameter while others use cross-validation
> makes the comparison meaningless.

## Designing the data-generating mechanism

Four questions, in order, take you from the application to a concrete generator.

**1. What is the object we need to create?** Look at the data you actually
analyze. For linear regression it is a covariate matrix $X$ and a response
vector $Y$. For a two-group test it is a matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$
with labels $Y \in \{0,1\}^n$. For PCA it is a matrix
$X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$.

**2. What models can create that object?** Look at the assumptions of the methods
being compared. Standard linear regression assumes
$Y = \beta_0 + X\beta_1 + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$.
PCA methods assume the data is well explained by $k \le \min(n,p)$ components,
$X = UDV^\top + E$ with $V^\top V = I$. Deliberately include models where the
assumptions *fail* --- correlated errors, a quadratic rather than linear mean, a
gamma rather than normal distribution.

**3. What parameters must be selected?** For linear regression: sample size $n$,
number of covariates $p$, the matrix $X$, the intercept $\beta_0$, the
coefficient vector $\beta_1$, and the noise standard deviation $\sigma$. Write
out the full list --- parameters left implicit become parameters chosen
arbitrarily.

**4. What do we expect the parameters to do?** This question demands the most
critical thinking and is the one most often skipped. For linear regression we
expect performance to improve as $n$ grows, as $\sigma$ shrinks, and as the
signal $\beta_1$ strengthens; and to degrade as $p$ grows. Writing these
expectations down before running anything turns the simulation into a genuine
test: results that contradict a well-reasoned expectation indicate either an
interesting phenomenon or --- more often --- a bug.

The method's own structure feeds back into the design. Sparse linear regression
additionally assumes some elements of $\beta_1$ are exactly zero, which implies
generating $\beta_1$ with exact zeros and considering both large-$n$/small-$p$
and small-$n$/large-$p$ settings.

## Choosing the settings

Fix a small number of complete settings --- **four to six at most** --- rather
than an unbounded grid. The discipline is to notice what is common across
settings and what differs, and to let the goal decide which differences matter.

A toy example, testing whether a mean equals 98.6 from a sample of size $n$:

| Setting | $n$ | $\mu$ | Distribution | What it probes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 100 | 98.6 | $N(\mu, 1)$ | $H_0$ true, normality holds |
| 2 | 100 | 99.6 | $N(\mu, 1)$ | $H_0$ false, normality holds |
| 3 | 100 | 98.6 | gamma, $\alpha\beta = \mu$ | $H_0$ true, normality violated |
| 4 | 100 | 99.6 | gamma, $\alpha\beta = \mu$ | $H_0$ false, normality violated |

: Four settings crossing truth of $H_0$ with validity of the normality assumption

These four settings do not cover all possible situations, and they are not meant
to. Here $n$ was held fixed at the size of the real data so that two factors that
matter more for the goal --- whether $H_0$ holds and whether normality holds ---
could each be examined. Choosing what *not* to vary is as much a design decision
as choosing what to vary.

> A study in which the author's preferred method wins in every setting is usually
> a study whose settings were chosen after seeing the results. Include at least
> one setting where the favored method is expected to struggle.

## How many replications?

The number of replications is a sample size and deserves justification rather
than a default of 1000. Each performance measure is estimated from `nrep`
replications and therefore has a **Monte Carlo standard error** (MCSE); for a
mean performance measure,

$$\text{MCSE} = \frac{\widehat{\text{SD}}}{\sqrt{n_{\text{rep}}}}$$

Invert this to plan. If pilot runs suggest $\text{SD} \approx 0.5$ and you want
to resolve differences of about $0.05$, then
$n_{\text{rep}} \approx (0.5/0.05)^2 = 100$ gives an MCSE of $0.05$ ---
marginal, since resolving a difference reliably wants an MCSE several times
smaller than the difference itself. The calculation takes two minutes and tells
you whether the study can answer its question at all.

Report MCSE alongside every headline number. Without it, readers cannot
distinguish a real difference from noise --- and neither can you.

> **Computing MCSE in code.** Always divide by `sqrt(nrep)` computed from the
> data rather than a hard-coded constant. Writing `sd(error)/10` works only while
> `nrep` happens to be 100, and will silently report wrong uncertainties the day
> you change it.

## Which performance measures?

Performance measures follow from the goal, and the useful discipline is to ask
what specifically the method is supposed to recover. Some measures will already
be produced by the method wrapper (classification accuracy, a rejection
decision); others need dedicated functions (quality of an estimated loading
matrix).

| Target | Measures |
|---|---|
| Estimation | Bias, empirical SE, RMSE, $\ell_1$ or $\ell_2$ error |
| Prediction | Test-set MSE, misclassification rate |
| Inference | Type I error control, power, coverage of nominal intervals |
| Selection | True/false positive rate for selected variables |

: Performance measures by target {tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

Two worked examples of the "what should it recover?" question:

*For a PCA study* --- how well is the true number of components $k$ recovered?
How well is the true loading matrix $V$ recovered? How closely is $X$
approximated by the recovered components? How well is new test data approximated?

*For a testing study* --- is Type I error controlled at the nominal level? Is the
null correctly rejected when the alternative is true? Is classification accuracy
high under the alternative? Are the right features selected (for sparse methods)?

Coverage and Type I error deserve emphasis: a method with small bias and badly
miscalibrated inference is not a good method, and only a simulation will reveal
the miscalibration.

# Implementation

## Project layout

Organize the repository so that clean, reproducible, well-commented code is
separated from exploration:

```
Functions/     data generation, method wrappers, metric functions
Simulations/   scripts that run the simulation
  Outputs/     saved raw results, one file per setting
Figures/       tables and figures produced from saved output
DataAnalysis/  scripts applying the chosen methods to the real data
Testing/       scratch work and exploration; no prescribed structure
README.md      what the study does and how to reproduce it
```

`Functions/` holds functions **only** --- no calls, no plots, no tests. Scripts
in `Simulations/` bring them in with `source("Functions/Methods.R")` and do the
calling. Mixing definitions with the code that exercises them is the fastest way
to make a project unreproducible, because sourcing the file then triggers
arbitrary side effects.

> Version control, repository setup, relative paths, and coding style are treated
> in the companion **reproducibility** materials; this guide covers only what is
> specific to simulations.

## Uniform interfaces

The single most important implementation rule: **functions of the same kind must
take the same inputs and return the same outputs**. This is what lets the
replication loop treat methods interchangeably, and what lets a fourth method be
added without touching the loop. On a team, it is also what lets four people
write code that composes.

### Data generation wrappers

*Input:* the setting. *Output:* a list containing the generated data and the
values of the true parameters needed to evaluate performance later.

The failure mode is subtle and expensive. Two teammates write:

```r
# Team member A
generateSim1 <- function(n) {
  # ... generate x with mean mu
  return(list(data = x, mean = mu))
}

# Team member B --- DIFFERENT names, DIFFERENT number of outputs
generateSim2 <- function(n) {
  # ... generate x with mean mu
  return(list(x = x, mu = mu, n = n))
}
```

Every downstream function must now be customized per setting. Agree on the
contract first, and both functions return `list(data = x, mean = mu)`.

Where settings share structure, use a master function with a shared sub-function
rather than repeating code:

```r
generateData <- function(setting) {
  if (setting == 1) {
    n <- 100; mu <- 98.6; distribution <- "normal"
  } else if (setting == 2) {
    n <- 100; mu <- 99.6; distribution <- "normal"
  } else if (setting == 3) {
    n <- 100; mu <- 98.6; distribution <- "gamma"
  }  # ... more settings
  x <- drawSample(n, mu, distribution)
  list(data = x, mean = mu)
}

drawSample <- function(n, mu, distribution) {
  if (distribution == "normal") {
    rnorm(n, mean = mu)
  } else if (distribution == "gamma") {
    rgamma(n, shape = 1, scale = mu)
  } else {
    stop("Unknown distribution")
  }
}
```

Keeping `n`, `mu`, and `distribution` as explicit arguments of `drawSample` means
a setting can be adjusted later without rewriting the generator. A practical team
workflow: divide the settings among members and write them as separate functions
first, then review each other's code together and refactor the shared structure
into sub-functions.

### Method wrappers

*Input:* the output of a data generation function. *Output:* either the
performance metrics directly, or the parameters from which performance can be
computed.

```r
# Classification study --- every method takes and returns the same things
applyKnn <- function(xtrain, ytrain, xtest, ytest) {
  # train the rule on (xtrain, ytrain)
  # evaluate accuracy on (xtest, ytest)
  # record which variables were used, for sparse methods
  list(accuracy = accuracy, ids = ids)
}

# PCA study
applySPCA <- function(X, k) {
  # loadings V (p by k) and scores (n by k), with Scores = XV
  list(V = V, Scores = Scores)
}

# A method that selects the number of components is a different contract
selectK <- function(X) {
  # returns a single integer
}
```

When a procedure wraps a method --- a permutation test, say --- pass the method
in as an argument so the wrapper works for all of them:

```r
permuteTest <- function(xtrain, ytrain, xtest, ytest,
                        alpha = 0.05, P = 100, method = applyKnn) {
  out <- method(xtrain, ytrain, xtest, ytest)
  accuracies <- rep(0, P)
  for (i in 1:P) {
    new <- reshuffle(xtrain, ytrain, xtest, ytest)
    outP <- method(new$xtrain, new$ytrain, new$xtest, new$ytest)
    accuracies[i] <- outP$accuracy
  }
  critical_a <- quantile(accuracies, probs = 1 - alpha)
  list(out = out, critical_a = critical_a,
       decision = out$accuracy > critical_a)  # TRUE means reject
}
```

With consistent contracts, generation and application compose without glue code:

```r
data    <- generatePCAdataSim1()
outK    <- selectK(data$X)
outSPCA <- applySPCA(data$X, outK)
```

### Metric functions

One small function per measure, plus a master `evaluate()` returning all measures
for a single replication:

```r
MSE <- function(yhat, Y) mean((yhat - Y)^2)

L1EstimationError <- function(hatbeta, truebeta) sum(abs(truebeta - hatbeta))

evaluate <- function(hatbeta0, hatbeta, truebeta, Y_test, X_test) {
  list("MSE Test" = MSE(yhat(hatbeta0, hatbeta, X_test), Y_test),
       "L1 Norm"  = L1EstimationError(hatbeta, truebeta))
}
```

## Randomness and saved output

Three practices specific to simulations cover most of the reproducibility risk.
(Version control and project setup belong to the reproducibility materials; what
follows is about randomness and results.)

**Set the seed in the script, once.** Record it in the file rather than typing it
at the console, so the script alone reproduces the run.

**Use a parallel-safe random number generator.** This is the pitfall that
silently invalidates results. Ordinary `set.seed()` does *not* make a parallel
`foreach` loop reproducible, because workers receive streams in a
non-deterministic order. The `doRNG` package solves this: `%dorng%` gives each
replication its own reproducible stream, so results are identical across runs
*and* across different numbers of workers.

```r
library(doParallel); library(doRNG)
cl <- makeCluster(detectCores()); registerDoParallel(cl)
set.seed(12345)

results <- foreach(i = 1:nrep, .packages = c("glmnet", "mnormt", "pls")) %dorng% {
  # ... one replication; the returned object is all that is kept
}
stopCluster(cl)
save(results, file = paste0("Simulations/Outputs/n", n_train, "p", p, ".Rdata"))
```

Note `.packages`: parallel workers start in fresh R sessions and do not inherit
your loaded libraries. Every package used inside the loop must be listed, and a
missing entry produces "could not find function" errors that appear only in
parallel, often after a long run.

**Save raw per-replication output, not summaries.** Simulations are expensive and
plots are not, so the replication script saves raw results and stops; a separate
script loads them and produces figures and tables. This makes new questions
("what does the *distribution* look like?", "is the mean driven by three
outliers?") answerable without recomputing anything, and you will redraw a figure
twenty times before the report is done. Name output files after the setting they
came from --- `n50p10.Rdata` --- so results are never ambiguous.

# Summary: reporting the results

**Show distributions, not just means.** Boxplots or violin plots across
replications reveal skewness, outliers, and occasional catastrophic failures that
a table of means hides entirely. A method that is best on average and fails badly
in 5% of replications is important to identify.

```r
pred_data.long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = method, y = error, fill = method)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(~ metric)
```

**Generate tables and figures from scripts, never by hand.** Point-and-click
export breaks reproducibility, and hand-typed numbers introduce errors that
nobody catches. Write the figure to a file and build tables programmatically.

**Use a consistent layout across settings.** Same method order, same colors, same
axis scales wherever comparison is intended. Readers compare panels visually, and
inconsistent scales make honest comparison impossible.

**Report failures.** Non-convergence, errors, and dropped replications are
results. State how many replications failed for each method and how they were
handled; quietly discarding them biases every number in the table.

**Give enough detail to reproduce.** State $n_{\text{rep}}$, the seed, the
software versions, and the parameter values for every setting. A reader should be
able to reconstruct the design from the report alone.

# Common pitfalls

| Pitfall | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Settings chosen after seeing results | Turns a study into a demonstration; fix the design in advance |
| Only favorable settings | Reviewers will find the missing case; better that you find it first |
| No expectations written down | Removes the check that would have caught the bug |
| Inconsistent wrapper input/output | Forces per-setting customization of everything downstream |
| Functions mixed with scripts and plots | Sourcing triggers side effects; nothing is reusable |
| No Monte Carlo SE | Differences cannot be distinguished from noise |
| Unfair tuning | Oracle-tuning one method invalidates the comparison |
| `set.seed()` with parallel loops | Results are not reproducible; use `doRNG` |
| Missing `.packages` in `foreach` | Fails only in parallel, often after a long run |
| Saving summaries only | Any new question requires re-running everything |
| Discarding failed replications silently | Biases results toward methods that fail on hard cases |
| Figures saved by point-and-click | Cannot be regenerated; breaks reproducibility |

: Pitfalls to avoid {tbl-colwidths="[40,60]"}

# Checklist {.unnumbered}

Before considering a simulation study finished:

- [ ] Goal stated with method type, specifics, and motivation
- [ ] Methods selected by literature search; each has an R implementation
- [ ] Tuning procedure specified and fair across methods
- [ ] Data-generating mechanism derived from the four design questions
- [ ] Four to six settings fixed, with the reason for each
- [ ] At least one setting where the favored method should struggle
- [ ] Expectations for each parameter written down before running
- [ ] Performance measures matched to what methods should recover
- [ ] $n_{\text{rep}}$ justified by a Monte Carlo SE calculation
- [ ] All wrappers of the same kind share input/output contracts
- [ ] `Functions/` contains function definitions only
- [ ] Seed set in-script; `doRNG` used if running in parallel
- [ ] Raw per-replication output saved, named by setting
- [ ] Figures and tables generated by script, not by hand
- [ ] Figures show distributions; tables report MCSE
- [ ] Failed replications counted and reported
- [ ] README explains how to reproduce every figure and table

# Appendix: generating structured random objects {.unnumbered}

Recipes that recur when building data-generating mechanisms.

**Random orthogonal matrix** ($p \times k$ with $V^\top V = I$):

```r
k <- 3; p <- 40
N <- matrix(rnorm(k * p), p, k)
V <- svd(N)$u[, 1:k]
round(crossprod(V), 2)   # identity
```

The `randortho` function in the `pracma` package does the same thing.

**Sparse unit-norm vector** ($s$ non-zeros in random positions):

```r
p <- 10; s <- 3
v <- c(runif(s), rep(0, p - s))
v <- sample(v)              # permute positions
v <- v / sqrt(sum(v^2))     # standardize to norm 1
```

**Sparse orthogonal loading matrix**, built column by column so orthogonality
holds:

```r
k <- 3; p <- 10; s <- 3
V <- matrix(0, p, k)
v <- sample(c(runif(s), rep(0, p - s)))
V[, 1] <- v / sqrt(sum(v^2))
for (j in 2:k) {
  v <- sample(c(runif(s), rep(0, p - s)))
  v <- v - tcrossprod(V[, 1:(j - 1)]) %*% v   # project out previous columns
  V[, j] <- v / sqrt(sum(v^2))
}
```

**Equi-correlation covariance matrix** --- more realistic than the identity:

```r
p <- 5; rho <- 0.7
Sigma <- matrix(rho, p, p) + diag(1 - rho, p)
```

**Data-driven covariance** --- estimate from real data and regularize slightly:

```r
Sigma <- cor(data)
Sigma <- 0.9 * Sigma + 0.1 * diag(ncol(data))
```

**Multivariate normal sample** with given mean and covariance:

```r
library(MASS)
X <- mvrnorm(n, mu, Sigma)
```

# Example project {#example-project .unnumbered}

A companion repository,
[`simulation-project-template`](https://github.com/IrinaStatsLab/simulation-project-template),
compares ridge regression, lasso, and principal component regression under a
linear model with correlated covariates. It is deliberately small enough to read
in one sitting, and demonstrates the separation of concerns, the uniform wrapper
interfaces, parallel replication with `doRNG`, saved raw output, and a separate
visualization script:

```
DataGeneration.R                   generate X and Y; generate a sparse beta
Methods.R                          applyRidge, applyLasso, applyPCR
Metrics.R                          MSE, L1 error, master evaluate()
n50_p10_parallel_replications.R    the experiment; saves n50p10.Rdata
Visualize_results.R                loads results, makes boxplots and a table
n50p10.Rdata                       saved raw per-replication output
Boxplots_comparison.pdf            the resulting figure
```

Because the project is small, the files sit in one flat directory rather than in
the `Functions/` and `Simulations/` folders of §5.1; the separation of concerns is
the same, and the folder layout becomes worthwhile as soon as a study has several
settings and multiple output files.

It is set up as a GitHub **template repository**: click *Use this template* to
create your own copy, then clone it and open the `.Rproj` file so that relative
paths resolve correctly. Replace the data generation functions with your
settings, the method wrappers with your methods, and the metric functions with
your performance measures. The replication and analysis scripts will need almost
no modification, which is the point of the uniform interfaces.

# Further reading {.unnumbered}

Morris TP, White IR, Crowther MJ (2019). Using simulation studies to evaluate
statistical methods. *Statistics in Medicine*, 38(11), 2074--2102.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.8086> --- the standard modern reference; source of
the ADEMP framework and detailed guidance on performance measures and Monte
Carlo error.

Burton A, Altman DG, Royston P, Holder RL (2006). The design of simulation
studies in medical statistics. *Statistics in Medicine*, 25(24), 4279--4292.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.2673> --- an earlier and still valuable treatment of
design choices.

Boulesteix AL, Groenwold RHH, Abrahamowicz M, et al. (2020). Introduction to
statistical simulations in health research. *BMJ Open*, 10(12), e039921.
<https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2020-039921> --- accessible introduction aimed
at applied researchers, with a useful treatment of performance metrics.

Sigal MJ, Chalmers RP (2016). Play it again: teaching statistics with Monte Carlo
simulation. *Journal of Statistics Education*, 24(3), 136--156.
<https://doi.org/10.1080/10691898.2016.1246953> --- simulation from a teaching
perspective, with the workflow laid out step by step.

Chalmers RP, Adkins MC (2020). Writing effective and reliable Monte Carlo
simulations with the SimDesign package. *The Quantitative Methods for
Psychology*, 16(4), 248--280. <https://doi.org/10.20982/tqmp.16.4.p248> --- a
framework-based alternative to hand-rolled simulation code in R.

Wilson G, Bryan J, Cranston K, Kitzes J, Nederbragt L, Teal TK (2017). Good
enough practices in scientific computing. *PLOS Computational Biology*, 13(6),
e1005510. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005510> --- project
organization, file naming, and data management habits that apply directly.
